title: How does your body change during pregnancy?
description: Pregnancy requires your body to adapt to support your pēpi's growth and development. This involves physical changes to your organs, changes in how your cardiovascular and immune systems function, and changes in hormone levels.

contentSections.title: Changes to organs in your body
contentSections.content:
Over the course of pregnancy, your womb increases in size and weight by about 10 times as pēpi grows within it. The blood vessels within the womb change size in the first half of pregnancy, becoming at least twice as wide by 20 weeks (~5 months). This ensures that the vessels can deliver increasing amounts of nutrient- and oxygen-rich blood to the placenta as pēpi begins to grow faster in the second half of pregnancy.

The pregnant womb takes up so much space in your body that it can cause your other organs to get pushed upwards. The space your lungs have for breathing is less. Your lungs become more efficient to help combat this.

When the womb pushes on your bladder, you may need to urinate more often. Pregnancy also puts extra load on the kidneys, which increases their activity and sometimes slightly increases their size to accommodate this.

Your breasts will grow in preparation for milk production, and your nipples may darken and enlarge. Your body temperature also rises during pregnancy due to increased progesterone levels and increased blood flow throughout the body.

Changes to the skin can also be seen. There are increases in pigmentation and stretch marks appearing, and a dark line called the 'linea nigra' appearing down the centre of the belly.

contentSections.title: Changes to how your body works
contentSections.content:
From early in pregnancy, your heart and blood vessels start to change. This means your heart can pump more blood to the womb. This means more oxygen and nutrients are carried to your pēpi.

By the end of the first trimester (first 12 weeks or 3 months), your heart rate will be beating faster (about 10%), and your blood pressure will be a little lower. You might notice that you feel your heartbeat more strongly, or that you are more likely to feel faint or dizzy after standing for a long time.

Over the rest of pregnancy, your body increases the total amount of blood you have by around 1.5 litres. This is important to ensure sufficient blood circulates to the placenta and to protect against blood loss during childbirth. As so much new blood is being produced, it is important to make sure you get your iron levels tested, as iron helps your blood cells carry oxygen to the placenta. Many people require extra iron in tablet form to ensure they and their pēpi have enough.

Your immune system also changes in pregnancy. Your pēpi and the placenta have a different genetic makeup from you. In pregnancy, your body has to change to 'tolerate' the placenta, which could otherwise be recognised as foreign to your immune system and attacked. The immune system is not 'turned down' though – it still operates well – but rather cells and factors released from your placenta teach it to accept your growing pēpi.

These adaptations (as shown below) help to support a healthy pregnancy.

contentSections.title: Changes to hormone activity in your body
contentSections.content:
Progesterone (often called the "pregnancy hormone") is first produced by the scar left behind in the ovary after it releases the egg (a structure called the corpus luteum). Progesterone plays an important role at the very start of pregnancy in maintaining the uterine lining (the endometrium) to support the early pregnancy "sticking". If your pregnancy started with IVF, you would have taken this hormone as a tablet.

The placenta also makes progesterone and becomes the main source of this hormone near the end of the first trimester, increasing its production throughout pregnancy as it grows.

Progesterone has important roles in changing the blood vessels in the womb to supply blood to the placenta, helping the thick muscle in your womb stretch to make way for pēpi, and in preparing your breasts to make milk.

Mum may experience some gastrointestinal issues, such as indigestion, diarrhoea, and constipation. Constipation, in particular, is linked to increased progesterone levels, which slow intestinal muscle contractions.

Estrogen is another hormone made by the placenta. Estrogen levels increase during pregnancy. Estrogen plays important roles in adapting your cardiovascular system to support pregnancy. It also helps the womb become more responsive to progesterone and promotes the growth of milk ducts in the breasts.

Increased estrogen can lead to thicker, shinier hair and reduce hair loss for mum, as the hair growth phase is prolonged. Estrogen can also lead to excessive hair growth around the body.

Due to pregnancy hormones, mum's nails may also change in the following ways: they may grow faster than normal, white dots may form on the nail surface, and grooves may form on the nail. Nails may also become brittle and break easily.
